Australian Logistics Firms Restore Operations After Cyber Attack Disruption

Australian transportation and logistics companies are returning to normal operations following a cyber attack last week that temporarily disrupted freight movement across the country. The incident, which began late Monday, targeted the IT systems of several major logistics providers, including Pacific Haulage Group and Southern Freightways, causing delays at ports and distribution centres.

The attack, described by company officials as a sophisticated ransomware campaign, led to the temporary shutdown of scheduling, tracking, and invoicing platforms. As a result, shipments were delayed, and some deliveries were rerouted or rescheduled, creating a backlog affecting customers nationwide.

“Within hours, our IT team identified unauthorised access and took our core systems offline as a precaution,” said Pacific Haulage Group’s Chief Executive, Tanya McIntyre. “We immediately engaged cyber security experts and worked closely with authorities to contain the breach and restore our services.”

By Thursday evening, most affected operations had resumed. McIntyre confirmed that no customer data appeared to have been compromised and that the company had not paid any ransom. “We restored systems from clean backups and are conducting a forensic review to ensure system integrity,” she said.

Industry representatives estimate that the disruption delayed an estimated 8,000 shipments and affected up to 15% of the country’s road and intermodal freight capacity during the peak of the incident. The Australian Logistics Association welcomed the swift response from affected companies but called for increased investment in cyber resilience.

“This attack highlights the vulnerability of our supply chains to cyber threats,” said Association President, Mark Ellison. “We urge firms to prioritise cyber preparedness as an essential part of business continuity planning.”

Union leaders echoed the call for greater cybersecurity training for frontline workers, noting that operational staff were among the first to notice irregularities in the systems. “Our members did exactly what they were trained to do—report suspicious activity and follow shutdown protocols,” said Transport Workers Union official Linda Chen.

Authorities have launched an investigation into the incident. The Australian Cyber Security Centre is working with impacted firms to strengthen defences and share lessons learned across the transportation and logistics sector.
